 Dengue cases in Aurora climb to 2,799
 By Leander C. Domingo
 October 24, 2026
 70
 Resize 
 Small 
 Medium 
 Large 
 BALER — Aurora province has logged 2,799 dengue cases as of Oct. 17, 2026 — more than double the 1,119 infections recorded in the same period last year — as health officials warn of continued transmission, particularly among children.
 The Provincial Health Office (PHO), led by Dr. Myrna Nicer, said its latest update on its official Facebook page added 77 new cases, bringing the cumulative total for the year to 2,799. Eight deaths linked to dengue have been recorded, with a case fatality rate of 2 percent.
 Patients ranged in age from 1 month to 104 years, with a median age of 12. Children aged 1 to 10 accounted for 1,174 cases, or 42 percent of all infections, indicating that younger age groups remain the most affected. Females comprised 1,407 cases, representing 50 percent of the total.
 By municipality, Maria Aurora logged the highest number of cases at 598, or 21 percent of the provincial total.
 Dilasag recorded the highest attack rate at 27.8 cases per 1,000 population, suggesting a more concentrated transmission in the northern town despite a smaller absolute count.

 The sharp year-on-year increase points to intensified transmission patterns in 2026, with cases more than doubling compared to last year.
 The age distribution, with a median of 12 and a large share among children, highlights exposure in household and school environments where daytime-biting mosquitoes are common.
 Advertisement 
 In response, the provincial government, through the PHO, has urged residents to intensify prevention measures under the 5S strategy.
 The strategy includes search and destroy of mosquito breeding sites, self-protection through the use of mosquito nets, insect repellents and long-sleeved clothing, and seeking early consultation at the first signs of dengue.
 It also covers support for fogging in outbreak areas where recommended by health authorities, and sustained hydration.
 The PHO stressed that prevention requires household and community participation, including regular cleaning of surroundings, removal of stagnant water, and prompt medical attention when symptoms such as fever, joint pain and rashes appear.
 Advertisement 
 Health officials continue to monitor transmission across the province and encourage collective action to reduce breeding sites and curb further spread.
